title: September 6–12, 1897
scope_note: Pilot week: 13 sourced items, centered on the September 6 anti-annexation mass meeting and the September 10–11 nūpepa record. This is still curated, not a complete ingestion of every paper published that week.

items.hawaiian: He aupuni kuokoa ko kakou i nai ia e na Kamehameha i moe aku la, a o ka pono kukulu Aupuni kuokoa a lakou i imi ai, oia ka kakou e hauoli nei i keia la, nolaila, he aha na pilikia i ulu ae i ko kakou noho kuokoa ana?
items.english_close: We have an independent government formed by the Kamehamehas. The right they sought to establish an independent government is why we have cause for happiness today. So what problems come from remaining independent?
items.feed_rendering: We already have an independent government. The Kamehamehas fought to build it. So tell me: what problem is our independence supposed to be causing?
items.voice_evidence: Kaulia frames independence as an inherited achievement, then ends by directly challenging the crowd with a question rather than merely stating a fact.
items.source_label: Kamakakoʻi, The Kaulia Speech: an excerpt from the Sept. 6, 1897 Palace Square address, later published in Ke Aloha Aina
items.translation_basis: Kamakakoʻi provides the Hawaiian excerpt and an English translation by Jacob Bryan Kaʻomakaokalā Aki and Noelani Goodyear-Kaʻopua.

items.hawaiian: O ke kuokoa a na makua Alii i imi ai i pono hooilina no ka lahui, oia ke ake ia nei e kanu ola ia, au e olelo ae ai ina e hoohuiia kakou me Amerika, oia ko kakou ae ana aku e kanu ola ia kakou ka lahui i loko o na popilikia he nui e hoea mai ana ma hope o ka hoohui ia ana.
items.english_close: The independence our Aliʻi sought as an inheritance for the lāhui is what they now seek to bury alive. Agreeing to annexation would be agreeing that the lāhui be buried alive in the hardships that would follow.
items.feed_rendering: They want to bury our independence alive. If we agree to annexation, we are agreeing to bury the lāhui alive with it.
items.voice_evidence: The source uses the repeated image of being buried alive, making this a deliberately vivid warning rather than neutral policy commentary.
items.translation_basis: Kamakakoʻi provides the Hawaiian excerpt and English translation.

items.hawaiian: A ihea kakou e noho ai? — I ka mauna!
items.english_close: Then where will we live? — In the mountains!
items.feed_rendering:
Kaulia: Then where are we supposed to live?
Crowd: In the mountains!
items.voice_evidence: The archival account preserves a direct question from Kaulia and an immediate shouted answer from the crowd. The exchange already behaves like a live reply thread.
items.source_label: UH Mānoa Library, The 1897 Petitions Protesting Annexation, account of the Sept. 6 Palace Square mass meeting
items.translation_basis: UH Mānoa preserves the exchange in English; the Hawaiian wording is also quoted in Noenoe K. Silva's Aloha Betrayed from the historical speech record.

items.hawaiian: Ina e mau ke kupaa o ka lahui me ke kue aku i ka hoohuiia o Hawaii me Amerika ke olelo nei au, e noke wale no ka Aha Senate o keia wahi Aupuni a helelei na paia pohaku o Iolani Hale, aole loa e hiki ke hoohuiia o Hawaii me Amerika.
items.english_close: If the lāhui remains steadfast in opposing annexation, the Senate of this government can keep trying until the stone walls of ʻIolani Palace fall, and Hawaiʻi still cannot be annexed to America.
items.feed_rendering: Stay together and keep refusing. They can argue in that Senate until the stone walls of ʻIolani Palace fall. We still do not have to consent.
items.voice_evidence: The speech uses the image of the palace walls falling before resistance gives way, supporting a defiant, endurance-focused rendering.
items.source_label: Noenoe K. Silva, Aloha Betrayed, quoting Kaulia's Sept. 6, 1897 speech
items.translation_basis: The scholarly source quotes the historical Hawaiian text and provides an English translation.

items.hawaiian: E lawe kakou i ke Kahua Hanohano o ka paio ana he lolo me ka lolo.
items.english_close: Let us take up the honorable field of struggle, brain against brain.
items.feed_rendering: Take the honorable field: brain against brain.
items.voice_evidence: The line is an imperative and a compact metaphor for political struggle through intellect rather than weapons.
items.source_label: Noenoe K. Silva, Aloha Betrayed, quoting Kaulia's Sept. 6, 1897 speech
items.translation_basis: The scholarly source quotes and translates the historical line.

items.hawaiian: Aole loa kakou ka lahui e ae e hoohuiia ko kakou aina me Amerika a hiki i ke Aloha Aina hope loa.
items.english_close: We, the lāhui, will never consent to the annexation of our land to America, down to the very last aloha ʻāina.
items.feed_rendering: We will not consent to annexation. Not while one aloha ʻāina is still standing.
items.voice_evidence: The line is a collective first-person refusal and is repeatedly cited as a defining declaration from the mass meeting.
items.source_label: UH Mānoa Library, The 1897 Petitions Protesting Annexation
items.translation_basis: UH Mānoa summarizes and translates Kaulia's declaration; the Hawaiian line is preserved in scholarship on the meeting.

items.hawaiian: Nolaila, mai makau, e kupaa ma ke Aloha i ka Aina, a e lokahi ma ka manao, e kue loa aku i ka hoohui ia o Hawaii me Amerika a hiki i ke aloha aina hope loa!
items.english_close: Therefore, do not be afraid. Stand firm in aloha for the land, unite in thought, and resist annexation until the very last aloha ʻāina.
items.feed_rendering: Do not be afraid. Stand firm. Stay together. Oppose annexation until the very last aloha ʻāina!
items.voice_evidence: Direct imperatives, repeated collective language, and the preserved exclamation mark support an urgent rallying tone.
items.source_label: Kamehameha Schools, ʻŌiwi leadership and aloha ʻāina, quoting Ke Aloha Aina, Sept. 11, 1897
items.translation_basis: Kamehameha Schools provides the historical Hawaiian line and English translation/context.

items.hawaiian: E hoomau ia ko kakou Kuokoa a i Aupuni Kuokoa malalo iho o kona mau Kanawai ponoi, nolaila, mai ae kakou e hoohuiia ko kakou Aina me Amerika.
items.english_close: Let our independence and independent government continue under its own laws. Let us not agree to join our land with America.
items.feed_rendering: Keep our independence. Keep our own government under our own laws. Do not agree to give the country away.
items.voice_evidence: The source moves from desired outcome to explicit instruction, using collective imperatives rather than detached description.
items.source_label: UH Mānoa teaching resource quoting James Kaulia in Ke Aloha Aina, Sept. 11, 1897
items.translation_basis: The resource supplies the Hawaiian passage and a close English translation.

items.hawaiian: E ke kanaka Hawaii aloha aina oiaio e nana aku oe i na mauna a mao aku, huli ae oe ma ka moana kai akea a nana aku a pau ka ike a kou mau maka, huli aku oe ma ka hikina a ka la i Kumukahi a me ka welona a ka la i Lehua, keia ka palena o na mokupuni o Ko Hawaii Pae Aina, kahi hoi a ko kakou mau kupuna i eha ai na ili i na Ihe Laumeki, e huli ana i pono oi ae no ka lakou mau mamo, oia kakou...
items.english_close: Hawaiian who truly loves the land, look to the distant mountains and across the ocean, from sunrise at Kumukahi to sunset at Lehua. These are the boundaries of the Hawaiian archipelago, where our ancestors suffered seeking greater rights for their descendants, who are us.
items.feed_rendering: Look at the mountains. Look across the ocean. From the sun rising at Kumukahi to the sun setting at Lehua: this is our pae ʻāina. Our ancestors fought for rights meant for us.
items.voice_evidence: Kalauokalani repeatedly tells the listener to look outward across named landmarks, then turns that view into a direct claim about inherited rights.
items.source_label: Kumu Pono Associates, quoting David Kalauokalani in Ke Aloha Aina, Sept. 11, 1897, p. 5
items.translation_basis: The study quotes the Hawaiian passage and provides a translation credited to Maly.

items.hawaiian: Hawaii Makemakeia no Roinia? He Kaeo Hoolewa Ki-paa!!
items.feed_rendering: Royalists are gathering for a mass meeting!!
items.voice_evidence: The source-facing transcription carries a question mark and double exclamation marks. The exact Hawaiian transcription remains under review, so the feed preserves visible intensity without inventing additional claims or slang.

items.translation_basis: The figure caption identifies the right-side headline as a mass meeting of royalists. Exact headline transcription should be checked against the primary scan before promotion beyond pilot status.
